projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Obed Oglesby was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Hi.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Hi. Oh, I'm sorry, go ahead.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: This is Lauren Smith. It's Sunday May 30th, 2004 in Ocala, Florida. It's Veterans Memorial Park and I'm interviewing this gentleman. And why don't you tell me your name and your date of birth and your--what--when--the service that you were in and the war that you were in and your rank and--

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: My name is Obed B. Oglesby.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: --we'll go from there.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: I started out in the service in the Army--in--on November the 24th 1940 and was in the service on Pearl Harbor Day 1941. I served in the Army for about--as an enlisted man for about three years. Then I went to flight training and was commissioned as a pilot in the U.S. Army Air Corp and I stayed as a career. I started out as a Private and I retired as Lieutenant Colonel. Other than that, I was born on the 20th of June 1922. So I'm now 81 and will be 82 next month.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: So tell me, you--you were drafted? And that--

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: I'm sorry, you enlisted and then you--

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Perhaps I should cover that because that's something that they seem to ignore in history.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Please explain.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: In the late 30's and 40's we had no Army. Period. We had about 50,000 men if my--if my statistics are correct. And at that time Europe was being torn up by Hitler and Mussolini and whoever happened to come along. So they decided that they had to build an army immediately. The draft was about to start, but those weren't trained men. The only calvary of trained men they had in the United States, other than the low regular army, was the Army National Guard, and within a two-month period in 1940 they called to active duty, federal duty, every guard unit in the United States and I was in the Missouri National Guard. The Show Me Regimen, 128th Field Artillery, and we went to Port Jackson, South Carolina, stayed there until after Pearl Harbor and were transferred down here as a regiment to Camp Bunding, Florida. And I had applied for flight training and been accepted and I went to flight training for Camp ___. I completed flight training, got my wings in April of 1943 and was convinced I was going off to combat to fight the Germans and they said, "No, you're not. You're going to be an instructor," and I said, "Oh, no, I'm not." And they said "Oh, yes, you are." So that's the way I ended up. Once the Air Corp Training Command got their hands on you, if you did your job reasonably well, they wouldn't let you go. I volunteered, I don't know how many times, to get out of instructing and go to combat. I was recommended to fly the B-38, the Lockheed Lightning, and never got to it.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Why would they want you to be an instructor and not combat?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: I don't know.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Because you were--because you were so good?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Well, they told us they only took the best, but I've heard that before too.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: So it was a compliment?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: They came down about a month before we got our wings up here in Dothan, Alabama and tried to get people to volunteer to be instructors and I know one man volunteered. The rest of us said, "No, we do not want to be instructors." But the morning that we got our wings they handed us our orders. That's exactly what it was and I spent two years there. They had numerous cavalry going out to combat and I volunteered for every one of them and never got on. Finally, they came down with a cavalry for B-17's 4-engine bomber and I volunteered for that and they finally let me go. I was in B-17 transition, almost through, when they dropped the atomic bomb. After that, I stayed for career because I liked it and I served in Korea and I served in Vietnam. So it was an interesting life in many ways, but in other ways it wasn't. If you got shot at, but then--when I retired I was in a Special Air Mission Squadron at O'Hare Field in Chicago. We were flying VIPs, Commanding General of the Continental Armies, mostly military, but quite a lot of civilian VIPs. Heads of industry and that sort of thing. I retired with 24 years and two months, I think, or three months, something like that.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Well, you have a lot to talk about for history. Do you--why don't we spend a little bit of time on each war; could we do that? And tell me some--tell me your most memorable experience about Japan and then Korea and then Vietnam. Maybe a little background about what you did, but then something memorable.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Well, as I said, I instructed. Built up a lot of flying hours before the war was over. In Korea, I flew in what they call the Liaison Squadron. We were flying in and out of the front lines, hauling causalities, hauling blood, anything that we could. We landed on beaches. We landed on roads. Anything we could get into to support the combat operation. In Vietnam, I went over as an advisor to the Vietnamese Air Force. I was one of the first people who went into Vietnam. I was there when the first two Americans were killed. We had numerous firefights, but they wouldn't admit that there was a war at that time and I was there when the first two were killed. Their names are the first two on the Monument in Washington. Rather an interesting country. I'd like to see Korea now because it was practically demolished when I was there and I understand it's a very progressive country now. I suppose Vietnam would be the same way if we still had control of it. Other than that, I can't think about too much except the times that students tried to kill me during World War II.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Tell me about that student.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Well, I had a student cut the engine off one night. We were night flying and we were idling and, of course, I couldn't tell the engine was cut off because the prop was still(?___+?)and we were gliding down to get into the traffic pattern to go around and he went below the traffic altitude--he had--they had given to him that night to fly because he was a weak student and they wanted to know what I thought of him, and we went down below traffic altitude and you could see the lights of the field over the top, and so when I applied the power to pull back up off the tree tops there wasn't any power. The airplane was dead. You didn't survive something like that. So I got us out of it and we weren't killed, but we were fortunate we weren't. I had a number of incidents like that. So many I can't even think about it to tell you the truth.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: What was your life like with your fellow pilots?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: What was just the average daily existence?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Oh, that was great.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Troop life. Everything.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Among your pilots you had a comradery I don't think that you had among other units. They brainwashed you. You saw above every door of the best damn pilots in the world and that kind of thing, and it really was an elite bunch of men. They--they were--I don't include myself in that, but they were--they were all pretty good physical specimens. Of course, you had to be to pass the physical to get into it. No, I wouldn't trade that life and what I went through there for anything in the world. The flying part of it. It just was something that you have to be in it to understand it. You really do.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Have--did you keep up with any of them after the wars?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: No, not really. You know, you were transferred so many times and people went here and people--I tried to check on a few of them on the Internet--I'm not an Internet person, but my daughter--step-daughter has tried to find some of them on the Internet, but we've never been successful. I knew a lot of ex-prisoners-of-war in Germany that I would like to talk to, but--

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: How--how did you know them?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Through--when they came back, when they were released. They--they had careers just like I did. They stayed in the Air Corp--

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: --and then they became Air Force in 1947. That's the only way. But I can't think of a greater bunch of men to associate with, very frankly.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Tell me--that--that you--did you ever have any causalities in your unit and--

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Oh yeah, that happened, that happened. I've told people we killed more people in training then they killed in Iraq so far. I mean, in accidents.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Wow, that's a good percentage.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Oh, it was. The airplanes we were flying were not as modern and sophisticated as the ones they have today. Yes, we did. I can't tell you any specific ones. Well, for example, the night the student turned the engine off on me, another instructor had been killed about the week before in broad daylight. The same thing. And I was at night where I couldn't see too much in the back cockpit.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Let's see. How did you--were you married at the time?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: I wasn't married then. I was just going to tell you--first thought--

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Okay, yeah, tell me--

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: First thought that runs through my mind--

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: --your family life.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: I was supposed to be married in about two weeks and the first thought--the first thought I had is wondering what she's going to say when they tell her I'm dead. Fortunately, they didn't have to tell her.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: So this was a sweetheart you already had back at home?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: No, I hadn't met her. I went through preflight at Montgomery Alabama--not an actual--was not an actual Air Force base. It was actually Southeastern and I met her while I was in preflight there at Montgomery and strangely enough they sent me right back to that same town as an instructor. It sounds suspicious, but it wasn't by choice, I'll tell you. Then we were married in October of 1943. She's now dead and I married again.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: How did you and your wife keep in touch while you were in World War II?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Mail. Once in a while--even the overseas long-distance lines were so--I can't think of a term to describe them, but they were so expensive and so bad that you just didn't do it. Mail was that--you always waited on that mail call and that was a big occasion.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Was it regular letters or victory mail or?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: No, it was regular letters. They were--they were--what's the term? The one they're using with the Library here. Escapes me. Anyhow, somebody read the letters and if there was anything in it that shouldn't be, they didn't let it come through.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Oh, someone would--

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: --censor--

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Censor. That's the term I'm trying to think of.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: --the mail that your wife would write or that you would write--

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Or that you would write, yeah--

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: --to make sure--

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: They made pretty sure you didn't put anything in there that wasn't supposed to be there.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Was there something special you did for good luck? Some ritual or were you faithful? Did you have--go--participate in church or did you have a Chaplain Service?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: The only thing I ever did for good luck--I had one of--my first wife--a handkerchief, and I carried it in my flight suit all the time.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Aww.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: And I wouldn't take it out. I left it in the--in the pocket of my flight suit and that was supposed to be my good luck charm.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Sweet. Did you--while you were stationed, did you take any side trips? Did you have any leave where you could travel and see--

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Oh, from Vietnam for example, I went to Hong Kong for part of the time and from Korea I went over to the Philippines. Well, I was stationed in the Philippines also. Forgot that. But--I had-- all my time was in the Orient. I never got to Europe.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: I had a chance to go to Cambodia and I didn't do it. I don't know why I didn't because the people who went to Angkor Wat, the ruins over there, said it was very, very interesting, but I didn't do it. But Japan I find to be a very interesting country.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: How so?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Oh, it's just--during World War II they would have us imagine it was a crude, lewd country, and it's not. It's a very developed country. The people I found very interesting. I hated to think that at one time their armed services were pretty brutal, but I really enjoyed. I tried to get my first wife to come to Japan. They told me that when I left Korea if I would stay in Japan for three years--if my wife and children would meet me on the docks in Japan when I got there and I could spend three years there with them, but she wouldn't come. She didn't think the kids would get enough education, things like that. Couldn't convince her, so I just gave up and came home. I would like to spend three years in Japan. It was that interesting to me.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: How--what was--what were the Japanese civilians like? Like did--

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Well, of course--

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: --you have much interaction?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: --we were the conquerors and they were the conquered so maybe that had some effect, but they were very, I thought polite, courteous, well-mannered. I wouldn't say that about Vietnam. The people were rather rude there, but--

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Interesting.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Japan was entirely different. It just was. I came back through there a couple times. Coming and going from overseas in addition to having spent some time there stationed over there.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: What was the food like in all the three places?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: I always liked it.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Did you?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Most people would complain about GI food and I said, "I don't know what they're complaining about, I like it." And I got along well.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: How did you--were mess halls set up? Or you had cooking--

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: No, we had--

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: --C-Rations sent over?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: No, we had our own mess halls. Of course, the officers always had an officers mess and an enlisted mess, but we had--we normally had cooks from the country we were in that took care of food.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Waitresses from the country. No I never--I complained about a lot of things, but the food wasn't one of them.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: So you were in the military 24 years, I think you said?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: What did you do when you retired from that?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Flew Corporate. I flew for Nobility Homes, located here in town for 17 years.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: They had their own airplane to fly their people around and fly customers in to--they built mobile homes.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: They had plants in Texas and North Carolina so I flew for another 24 years after I retired from the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Well--

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: So I liked to say I bored a lot of holes in the sky because I did.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: That worked well. Did you keep in touch with any aspect of military life when you retired? Did you--are you in a VSO or--

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Well, I'm a member of what was the Retired Officers Association.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: MOAA now.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Yeah. MOAA, I'm a member of that. I have been for, I guess, close to 30 years.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Oh, okay. I'll have to write that down.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: In fact, having something here at the Veteran's Park, I think, tomorrow or the next day or they're participating. I'll say it that way. That's--other than going to Air Force Bases and that sort of thing, that's about the extent of my activity. I've never belonged to America Legion, for which my father would be greatly disappointed, because he was a Legionnaire from the word "go".

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: But I--I had an uncle killed in World War II--World War I. And my dad was a veteran of World War I, but I've never belonged to America Legion or VFW or any of those other organizations.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Did you--what was I going to ask? Ever take advantage of the GI Bill or--or--

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: --or the home loans or any--

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: I took advantage of both those. I went to college for two years after I retired and I bought a home out in Texas using the GI Bill, just the one time. I think that was a great program for us. It really was. For a lot of people. Especially the guys who came home directly after World War II and went to college. It really did something for a lot of people. That was the greatest reward, I think, they could have given those men for--

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: There is something I was going to ask you. Oh, did you--when you were in any of the Asian countries, ever have visitors for entertainment, like from the USO or?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Sure. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Tell me something about that.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Well, I can't remember anybody by name. But in the Philippines, for example, we had a troupe, and in Korea. But I can't remember the names of the people who did it. Of course, Bob Hope was the big name. I had a guy who worked for me in the Air Force who flew Bob Hope's troupe for a little while.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Neat.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: He thought it was quite a--quite a thing.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: That would be. What? Did they sing and have comedy skits or dancing or?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: They took you back a little bit to home. It was like seeing something that a-- that's one thing that--homesickness, I think, is one of the biggest things that a GI has to put up with. The land of the Big PX we called it. To get back to the land of the Big PX. That meant going home.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: That makes sense. Did--did the Red Cross or any organization have--ever have parties or dances--

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: --or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: I never saw anything. I did see some going ashore in some of the foreign ports. I did see them handing out different things. I didn't smoke so they didn't hand me any cigars or cigarettes. Yes, they were visible. I don't mean that, but just something I didn't partake in.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Did you feel scared, or what did--how did you feel ever?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: After--you were in some dangerous parts--

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: You always knew the danger was there. But no, I didn't really.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: What would--what would be going through your mind during these years?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Well, sometimes when you were flying there were things going through your mind that could happen to you. But I remember one beach that I landed on in Korea. They never knew whose hands it was in when we landed. We always landed with one hand on our .45 and the other hand on the throttle to get got out of there if somebody--and it was above the Yellow River, the line that they used as demarcation between North Korea and South Korea. And then, one time, I remember going up to an island to pick up some agents and they told me they didn't know which side. They thought that maybe they were double agents so be very careful. And you wondered what you'd do if one of them blazed up and put a gun on--to the back of your head and said let's go to North Korea. But nothing like that ever happened. Those--those were a little bit worrisome. And then in Korea we had what we called Bed Check Charlie. Was always coming down and dropping bombs to see if he could disturb our slumber.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: You are a walking history book. It's wonderful. Well, that's great because your memory will be part of the Library of Congress's record so children--school children a hundred years from now will--

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Well, I think they should.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: --benefit from your interview.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: I really do. I was saying this morning, that's where I'm coming from, church. That's why I'm dressed--

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Is it nice?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: They asked for anybody who was a Veteran for World War II only to stand up ___+ and I couldn't see for sure because I was in the--almost the front pew, but somebody told me later on there was only about 50 of us stood up and that's a congregation of probably 1500 people. So--

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: --that tells you something. And then they mentioned the fact that so many of us are dying. Eleven hundred a day, I think the paper said this morning. Four million left, out of 16 million of us.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Well, is there anything else you'd like to add, Mr. Oglesby?

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Three wars and saving people from tyranny, different times.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: Life--life seems kind of dull anymore. Yeah, but first in the--in the Gulf War--my second wife at first knew nothing about my life in the service because we weren't married at the time, and that night I was watching television and the guys were going down the strip giving the universal signal to the guys on the line and she said she never saw anything like that. She said, "You were up facing the floor and going back and forth" And I said, "Well, my brotherhood was going to war", and for first time since 1940 I wasn't there, so that bothered me.

sp.speaker: Lauren Smith
sp.p: Well, thank you very much.

sp.speaker: Obed Oglesby
sp.p: You're very welcome.
